Electrical discharge machining of Hastelloy alloys is sensitive to the physical and microstructural properties of the electrode material, which influence process efficiency, machining accuracy, and surface roughness. Nowicki et al. report that graphite is increasingly used for EDM electrodes because of low raw material cost, good machinability, and high sublimation temperature, and that grain size markedly affects material removal rate (MRR), tool wear rate (TWR), and surface roughness (Ra) in EDM of Hastelloy C-22. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Their experiments with POCO graphite grades (1 µm AF-5 and 10 µm S-180) show larger-grain graphite gives higher process efficiency but higher relative tool wear, whereas finer-grain graphite yields the lowest Ra. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

A later study by the same group frames the grain-size effect as a challenge for industrial implementation but reports that fine-grained graphite increases process efficiency and reduces tool wear in EDM of Hastelloy C-22; detached graphite grains are observed to disturb discharge stability and process efficiency. (Nowicki et al. 2024) Both studies derive empirical or mathematical models linking machining parameters and electrode grain size to technological indicators and surface texture, enabling prediction of machining outcomes under the tested conditions. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Across EDM studies of high-performance alloys, discharge energy parameters—peak current and pulse duration—consistently emerge as dominant drivers of MRR, TWR, and surface finish. Nowicki et al. identify discharge current and pulse duration as the main factors controlling MRR and Ra for both graphite grades, and time interval as dominant for relative electrode wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Ramabalan et al. likewise find current and pulse duration strongly affect electrode wear, taper, and profile changes (e.g., transformation of sharp edges toward hemispherical ends) in EDM of Hastelloy B2. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) Experimental design and ANOVA analyses in other alloy studies corroborate the primacy of peak current (amperage) for MRR, TWR, and Ra outcomes. (Nas & Kara 2022)(Akıncıoğlu 2022)

A range of adjunct process modifications aim to mitigate high TWR and low MRR inherent to EDM. Reviews and experimental reports summarize strategies including cryogenic treatment, powder-mixed dielectric, ultrasonic assistance, and electrical-discharge coating to improve MRR, reduce TWR, or modify surface integrity; these works discuss effects on MRR, TWR, Ra, and recast layers and identify gaps for further research. (Shastri et al. 2022)(Liew et al. 2020) For example, Taguchi-based optimization found cryogenic treatment type, pulse-on time, and peak current jointly determine optimal Ra and MRR in a corrosion-resistant superalloy, with peak current explaining the largest share of variance. (Nas & Kara 2022) Studies on nanopowder-mixed EDM and electrode cryogenic treatment report substantial reductions in electrode wear and overcut for brass electrodes under specific dielectric conditions, illustrating that electrode treatment and dielectric additives can strongly influence electrode life and dimensional accuracy. (Sana et al. 2024)

Despite these findings for graphite and for process variants, direct comparisons between composite electrodes and conventional electrodes (graphite, copper, brass) specifically in EDM of Hastelloy alloys are not represented in the supplied literature.

Graphite electrode grain size strongly controls EDM outcomes on Hastelloy C-22, with finer grains reducing tool wear and coarser grains increasing process efficiency at the cost of higher relative tool wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

Experimental comparisons using POCO AF-5 (1 µm) and POCO S-180 (10 µm) show that coarser graphite yields higher material removal rate while finer graphite produces lower surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

A complementary study that also tested AF-5 and EDM-180 reported that fine-grained graphite increases process efficiency and reduces tool wear, and that detached graphite grains influence discharge stability and removal mechanisms. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Both studies modelled the dependence of machining indicators on electrical parameters and concluded that discharge current and pulse duration are the principal controls of MRR and Ra for the graphite grades tested. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Relative tool wear of graphite electrodes is reported to be dominated by the time interval between discharges in the experiments on Hastelloy. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

Across nickel-based and other difficult-to-machine alloys, peak current (amperage) appears repeatedly as the most influential parameter on MRR and tool wear, with ANOVA results attributing the largest share of variability to current in Taguchi-designed experiments. (Nas & Kara 2022)(Akıncıoğlu 2022)

Process instability at sharp electrode features promotes shape degradation and increased wear: square electrodes developed hemispherical ends when sparks became unstable, indicating that current and pulse duration govern wear-driven geometry change. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)

Broader reviews of EDM interventions identify multiple approaches—cryogenic treatment, powder-mixed dielectric, ultrasonic assistance and others—that modify MRR, TWR and surface integrity, and which represent potential routes to mitigate high tool wear and roughness. (Shastri et al. 2022)

Nanopowder in the dielectric and cryogenic treatment of electrodes have been reported to reduce electrode wear and improve dimensional accuracy in other alloys, suggesting similar strategies could be explored for Hastelloy EDM. (Sana et al. 2024)

Electrical discharge coating (EDC) is noted as an adjacent technology for producing modified surface layers via discharges, but its direct relevance to electrode selection in EDM of Hastelloy is not established in the cited literature. (Liew et al. 2020)

Selective laser melting (SLM) produces near-fully dense maraging-steel components by layer-wise melting and rapid solidification, a process that promotes unique microstructural features compared with conventional routes. (Yap et al. 2015) The as-built SLM microstructure is reported as a fine martensitic matrix with submicron grain sizes and abundant needle-shaped nanoprecipitates Ni3X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) in some studies, which is attributed to extremely high cooling rates during fabrication. (Tan et al. 2018) Ahmadkhaniha et al. observed a fine-grain martensitic structure in as-printed maraging steel with no preferred texture or anisotropy across build sections and a surface roughness Ra ≈ 10 µm. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Heat treatments applied to SLM maraging steels modify these as-built features by promoting precipitation, relieving residual stress, and—in some regimes—reverting martensite to austenite. Tan et al. applied heat treatments chosen from phase-transformation temperatures and found that aging produces massive needle-shaped Ni3X precipitates responsible for age hardening, while the treatments significantly relieve residual stress and slightly reduce mechanical anisotropy. (Tan et al. 2018) Godec et al. investigated the interaction of prior solution treatment and aging with subsequent plasma nitriding and reported that thermochemical treatment following prior heat treatment improves wear and corrosion resistance relative to nitriding without prior aging, where cracks in the compound layer occurred. (Godec et al. 2021) Ahmadkhaniha et al. compared SLM and wrought maraging steels in as-printed, austenitized/quenched and aged conditions, and concluded that despite the finer SLM microstructure, nano-hardness and corrosion behaviour in heat-treated conditions were similar to conventional wrought material, with precipitation playing a primary role in both hardness and corrosion potential. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Khan et al. tempered SLM maraging steel in the intercritical α' + γ range near 720°C to induce reversed austenite, finding that reversed austenite nucleates mainly at martensite lath boundaries where local Ni enrichment occurs due to intermetallic dissolution. (Khan et al. 2022) Electrochemical testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl showed the 720°C-tempered specimen—containing reversed austenite—exhibited higher pitting potential, lower corrosion current density and lower corrosion rate than as-printed, aged, and homogenized specimens without reversed austenite; the authors conclude reversed austenite enhances pitting resistance in chloride solution. (Khan et al. 2022)

Reviews of AM steels synthesize these findings and highlight both advantages and remaining challenges: AM induces hierarchical (sub)grains and fine precipitates that can enhance strength, wear and corrosion resistance compared with conventional steels, while achieving acceptable ductility and fatigue remains problematic and in situ phase transformations during AM act as intrinsic heat treatments that influence final properties. (Haghdadi et al. 2020) Afkhami et al. similarly note that heat treatment, build orientation and surface quality are influential parameters for performance of SLM steels, indicating gaps remain in comprehensive understanding of property interrelations. (Afkhami et al. 2019)
rows.b:
Selective laser melting (SLM) of 300‑grade maraging steel produces an ultra-fine martensitic matrix with submicron grains and dense populations of nanoscale Ni3X precipitates that arise from very high cooling rates. (Tan et al. 2018)

The SLM process builds parts layer by layer by selectively melting metallic powder with a high power‑density laser, and it is reported to produce near–full‑density components reaching up to 99.9% relative density. (Yap et al. 2015)

Because SLM imposes repeated rapid thermal cycles, it can act as an intrinsic heat treatment that triggers in situ tempering, precipitation and other phase transformations in precipitation‑hardening steels. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Microstructural characterization across multiple build planes of SLM maraging steel finds a fine martensitic structure with little evidence of a preferred crystallographic texture or anisotropy in grain morphology. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Measured average subgrain sizes of around $0.31\ \mu$m indicate cooling rates on the order of $10^{7}\ \mathrm{K/s}$ in optimised SLM builds. (Tan et al. 2018)

In the as‑built condition SLM maraging steels contain dense, needle‑shaped nanoprecipitates (Ni3Ti, Ni3Al, Ni3Mo) within the martensitic matrix, and these precipitates account for subsequent age hardening. (Tan et al. 2018)

Heat treatments applied according to detected phase transformation temperatures modify residual stress, precipitate state and mechanical anisotropy: aging increases hardness while reducing residual stresses and slightly reducing orientation‑dependent mechanical differences. (Tan et al. 2018)

Comparisons between heat‑treated SLM and conventionally produced maraging steels show that, despite the finer as‑built microstructure, nano‑hardness and corrosion behaviour after appropriate heat treatment can be similar between SLM and wrought material. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Aging produces the maximum nano‑hardness and corresponds to the lowest measured corrosion potential in the studies that compared as‑printed, austenitised/quenched and aged conditions, indicating precipitation strongly influences both hardness and electrochemical response. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Targeted intercritical tempering that induces martensite‑to‑austenite reversion deposits reversed austenite primarily along martensite lath boundaries, with local nickel enrichment from dissolved intermetallics promoting reversion nucleation. (Khan et al. 2022)

Specimens tempered at an intercritical condition near $720\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ that developed reversed austenite show higher pitting potentials and lower corrosion current densities in 3.5 wt% NaCl than as‑printed, aged, or homogenized specimens lacking reverted austenite. (Khan et al. 2022)

Thermochemical nitriding performed at $520\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for 6 h can be combined with prior solution treatment and aging, but nitriding without prior aging produced cracks in the compound nitride layer of SLM maraging steel. (Godec et al. 2021)

When nitriding follows prior heat treatment, the thermochemical treatment provides wear and corrosion resistance benefits relative to untreated SLM material, though origins of nitride layer cracks and pores are identified and discussed. (Godec et al. 2021)

SLM maraging steel composites containing WC reinforcements achieve higher densification and lower porosity than some alternative AM routes, and this densification correlates with improved wear performance in comparative studies. (Yan et al. 2018)

Despite many reported performance enhancements obtained through process control and post‑processing, gaps remain in understanding fatigue and other service‑condition behaviours of SLM steels due to the large parameter space of the process. (Afkhami et al. 2019)

The literature identifies upfront cost and affordability as central barriers to household rooftop solar adoption, with multiple studies reporting that high initial investment deters potential adopters. Khare et al. describe major constraints that hamper renewable energy development in India, framing cost as a key obstacle despite the country's favorable solar resource. (Khare et al. 2013) Tanveer et al. report that solar PV cost has a negative effect on consumers’ willingness to adopt in their sample, reinforcing the role of price as a direct inhibitor. (Tanveer et al. 2021) Aarakit et al. find affordability to be the main driver of the type of solar product adopted and show that flexible payment mechanisms significantly increase uptake among income-constrained households. (Aarakit et al. 2021)

Public subsidies and other policy incentives are repeatedly identified as important motivators that can overcome the initial investment risk and improve adoption rates. Parsad et al. find that government subsidies act as a primary motivator that helps overcome the initial risk of investing in rooftop PV systems and that financial motivators such as low prices and maintenance costs mitigate long-term apprehensions about returns. (Parsad et al. 2020) Goel documents national-level targets and policy ambitions for solar, specifying that India aims to reach 100 GW of solar capacity with 40 GW from grid-connected rooftop PV, indicating a strong policy focus on rooftop deployment. (Goel 2016) Several overviews of India’s renewable sector note that strong government support and policy instruments have been designed to attract investment and scale deployment. (J & Majid 2020)

Awareness, knowledge, and technical concerns emerge as non‑financial inhibitors that interact with economic barriers. Parsad et al. report that technical barriers and knowledge and awareness factors play a significant role in forecasting household investment decisions, with these factors ranked among the significant predictors in their models. (Parsad et al. 2020) Kappagantu et al.’s survey of a smart-grid pilot project in Puducherry explicitly examines consumer experience, roof-space considerations, and perceived barriers, indicating that user-level perceptions and local implementation issues affect willingness to adopt rooftop systems. (Kappagantu et al. 2015) Sovacool et al. highlight broader justice and equity-related concerns associated with household solar adoption, suggesting that social and spatial inequities may compound informational and accessibility barriers. (Sovacool et al. 2022)

Institutional and policy barriers include implementation challenges, heterogeneity in regional deployment, and gaps between ambitious national targets and on-the-ground uptake. Goel discusses India's ambitious solar targets alongside issues and challenges in achieving them, implying that policy ambition does not automatically translate into adoption without addressing implementation barriers. (Goel 2016) Reviews of India’s renewable sector identify a range of obstacles and recommend policy measures to address them, underscoring that institutional design and regulatory clarity matter for scaling rooftop PV. (J & Majid 2020) At the same time, cross-country evidence shows heterogeneity: Aarakit et al. find that rural residence and flexible payment schemes shaped adoption patterns in Uganda, illustrating that geographic and socioeconomic context modifies how institutional levers perform. (Aarakit et al. 2021)

Synthesis and gaps: studies converge on a multifaceted barrier set where upfront cost, limited financing options, subsidies, awareness, technical concerns, and institutional implementation jointly shape household rooftop PV decisions. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Tanveer et al. 2021)(Aarakit et al. 2021) However, evidence specific to rural Indian households’ adoption dynamics—linking these barriers empirically at the village or rural household level—is not present in the provided sources.

Randomized and pragmatic trials report mixed evidence on glycaemic outcomes associated with diabetes self-management apps. A multicentre pragmatic randomized controlled trial of the BlueStar app found no difference between intervention and control arms for the primary outcome of HbA1c at 3 months in the intent-to-treat analysis. (Agarwal et al. 2018) An exploratory analysis within the trial, however, associated greater individual app engagement with modest HbA1c reductions, estimating a $0.016$-point decrease in 3-month HbA1c for each additional day of app use in a subset of participants. (Agarwal et al. 2018) These results indicate that effect on glycaemic control in trials may depend on actual usage rather than allocation alone. (Agarwal et al. 2018)

Smaller or pilot evaluations demonstrate more proximal effects on self-management behaviours that are plausibly antecedent to glycaemic change. In a 12-week pilot of a user-centred, gamified app for adolescents with type 1 diabetes, daily frequency of blood glucose measurement increased by 50% during the pilot period, and participant satisfaction was high, though the authors noted that demonstrating HbA1c improvements would require larger, longer studies. (Cafazzo et al. 2012) Systematic syntheses across health behaviours similarly find that a majority of included app studies report statistically significant behavior change, and retention in intervention groups is often moderate to high (reported retention 60%–100%, with many studies ≥65%), but the body of evidence shows risk of bias and calls for larger, higher-quality trials. (Zhao et al. 2016)

Across qualitative and evaluative studies, recurring features are linked to sustained adoption and engagement: user-friendly design, low time burden, real-time feedback, individualized content, credible information and health professional involvement. (Zhao et al. 2016) Focus-group research identified nine user-centred themes including motivators, personalized guidance, tracking for awareness, credibility, goal setting, reminders, and concerns about sharing personal information, which map to established behaviour-change constructs. (Peng et al. 2016) Interviews with people living with type 2 diabetes emphasise that clinician recommendation and positive clinician–app interactions facilitate uptake, while lack of awareness, perceived disease severity, and limited technological or health literacy impede use. (Jeffrey et al. 2019)

App inventories and content analyses reveal mismatches between available apps and the functional needs for long-term self-management: many commercial apps emphasise reporting and reminders over personalized education or therapeutic decision support, and only a minority include comprehensive self-management feature sets. (Izahar et al. 2017) Concerns about app quality, data standards, security, and the need for certification recur in the literature and are presented alongside calls to educate consumers and develop better quality-assurance mechanisms. (Boulos et al. 2014)

Taken together, the evidence shows consistent associations between specific engagement-supporting features and both short-term behaviour change and higher retention, but inconsistent translation into HbA1c benefits at the trial level, likely because effects depend on sustained, contextualised use that many studies do not achieve or measure adequately. (Zhao et al. 2016)(Agarwal et al. 2018)(Peng et al. 2016)

Empirical evidence on business growth among women who access microfinance or related interventions is mixed but offers clear patterns about what facilitates enterprise expansion. A seven-year quasi-experiment in rural India found that an ICT intervention substantially increased business creation—160 new businesses in treatment villages versus 40 in controls—and that social network position interacted with ICT use to raise entrepreneurial activity and profits for women with strong ties to family and community. (Venkatesh et al. 2017) Complementing this, a mixed-method study reported that female entrepreneurs supported by microfinance are better off economically than non-entrepreneurs, indicating gains in business-related outcomes for participants. (Khan et al. 2022) These findings imply that finance combined with information, technology, and enabling social conditions associates with stronger enterprise growth than credit alone. (Venkatesh et al. 2017)(Khan et al. 2022)

Studies that examine empowerment and household decision-making stress that empowerment has multiple dimensions and that interventions affect these dimensions unevenly. A Three-Dimensional Model distinguishes micro-level (personal), meso-level (relational), and macro-level (societal) empowerment, and emphasizes that time and culture shape when and which dimensions change following interventions. (Huis et al. 2017) Empirical work aligns with this: the mixed-method study found improvements across economic, psychological, and to a lesser extent social and political indicators for women entrepreneurs, while noting relatively smaller impacts in political empowerment and modest social gains. (Khan et al. 2022) Qualitative research on social entrepreneurship in North India further shows that business processes designed to fit local norms can empower women while contributing to gradual change in the social order, suggesting pathways from individual economic activity to shifts in household and community relations. (Haugh & Talwar 2014)

However, several sources caution that credit by itself is insufficient and can have adverse effects without complementary supports. An ethnographic study in Bangladesh reported that microfinance sometimes increased indebtedness and exacerbated economic and social vulnerabilities in poor communities, highlighting risks when market-based credit is not accompanied by safeguards or other forms of support. (Banerjee & Jackson 2016) At the institutional level, reviews of the microfinance industry underline that market forces and the push toward profitability change which clients are served, and that institutions with strong social missions—often supported by subsidies—are better positioned to reach the poorest. (Cull et al. 2009) Broad reviews of the field also stress the need to integrate finance scholarship with impact assessment and managerial practices to understand when microfinance produces sustainable, pro-poor outcomes. (Brau & Woller 2004)

Despite these insights, direct, consistent evidence on how microfinance-mediated enterprise gains translate into concrete shifts in intra-household decision-making (e.g., control over income, time allocation, bargaining outcomes) across contexts is sparse.
rows.b:
Microfinance-supported entrepreneurship can raise women's economic and psychological indicators of empowerment, but effects on social and political dimensions are smaller and uneven. Khan et al. find that female entrepreneurs financed through microfinance score higher than non-entrepreneurs on economic, social, political and psychological measures of empowerment, while noting that political and—especially—social empowerment show relatively smaller gains. (Khan et al. 2022)

Empowerment through entrepreneurship often interacts with local social and cultural norms, which both constrain and shape the forms of agency women can exercise; business models that adapt to those norms can nonetheless shift social order over time. (Haugh & Talwar 2014) Entrepreneurship initiatives that align with prevailing norms may therefore prompt both individual gains and gradual social change. (Haugh & Talwar 2014)

Interventions beyond credit—such as information and communication technology (ICT) and network-building—amplify entrepreneurial take-up and, in some contexts, profits. (Venkatesh et al. 2017) In a seven-year quasi-experiment, villages receiving an ICT intervention generated 160 new businesses compared with 40 in control villages, and the combination of high community centrality and ICT use produced the highest levels of entrepreneurial activity and success. (Venkatesh et al. 2017)

However, market-based microfinance can also produce adverse economic and social outcomes when not paired with broader support, as rising indebtedness and weakened social capital have been documented in ethnographic work. (Banerjee & Jackson 2016) This suggests credit alone may impose risks that offset or limit its empowerment potential unless accompanied by complementary measures. (Banerjee & Jackson 2016)

The literature on microfinance institutions and their objectives further clarifies why outcomes vary: some institutions pursue social missions supported by subsidies, while others move toward commercial models, and these organizational choices affect which clients are served and how programs are delivered. (Cull et al. 2009) A broad review of microfinance scholarship highlights diverse topics—sustainability, client targeting, products, regulation and impact assessment—underscoring heterogeneity in programs and evidence. (Brau & Woller 2004)

Conceptual frameworks that distinguish dimensions and timing of empowerment help explain mixed empirical results; one model separates personal, relational and societal empowerment and emphasizes that culture and the time lag between intervention and evaluation shape where and when effects appear. (Huis et al. 2017) The model implies that program designers should specify which empowerment dimension they target and when they expect to observe change. (Huis et al. 2017)

Studies of women-led social enterprises show that combining commercial and transformational goals can yield community-level impacts, suggesting sector- and context-specific design matters for wider development effects. (Kimbu & Ngoasong 2016)

Household-level studies identify four recurrent frictions between awareness and installation: informational gaps, procedural complexity, structural limitations, and perceived financial risk. (Bagla 2026)

Bagla’s qualitative study in Karnataka used semi-structured interviews and questionnaires with 70 households to probe the “last mile” frictions that prevent subsidy uptake, and triangulated findings with national survey evidence. (Bagla 2026) Bagla reports that non-adopters rank space and roof-ownership constraints as the leading barrier, followed by information gaps and upfront cost, while adopters rate environmental concern as their primary motivation. (Bagla 2026) The study quantifies a notable divergence between anticipated and experienced procedural burden: adopters expected installation complexity at a mean of $5.1$ out of $10$ before installation but reported actual complexity of $2.2$ after installation. (Bagla 2026) Bagla also documents a “subsidy paradox” in which restrictions on panels, vendor empanelment, and paperwork dilute the practical value of capital subsidies, and notes that $45.8\%$ of adopters stated they would have adopted even without the subsidy. (Bagla 2026)

Studies from other Indian states and international case studies corroborate and nuance these themes. N.M & A.H apply the Theory of Planned Behaviour in North Kerala using a structured questionnaire and structural equation modelling, and find that environmental concern, government subsidy awareness, and cost–benefit perception positively affect attitudes toward rooftop solar; attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control then significantly influence installation intention, with the structural model explaining $30.3\%$ of attitude variance and $26.8\%$ of intention variance. (N.M & A.H 2026) Panwar & Yadav’s survey in Meerut similarly highlights cost, environmental consciousness, government incentives and technological reliability as salient determinants of household perception and reports that adoption remains below desired levels. (Panwar & Yadav 2026)

Quantitative and theory-driven work links perceived product attributes to purchase intention. Kumar & Kaushik use diffusion of innovation dimensions with data from $863$ respondents and structural equation modelling to show that relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, innovativeness and observability positively influence purchase intention, while trialability does not. (Kumar & Kaushik 2022) Kumar’s Patna study employed a $200$-respondent questionnaire and factor analysis to identify context-specific barriers that require collaboration among government, providers and the public. (Kumar 2025) Outside India, Chidembo et al.’s village case studies used purposive sampling and thematic network analysis to find that rural households often perceive solar PV as cheap and environmentally friendly but simultaneously express doubts about energy quality, theft risk, and high capital requirements, motivating calls for awareness programmes and inclusive financing. (Chidembo et al. 2022)

Across studies, two patterns emerge: (1) subjective perceptions of complexity, cost and reliability shape intention strongly, and (2) procedural and structural constraints—roof ownership, vendor rules and paperwork—can erode the effective value of subsidies. (Bagla 2026)(Kumar & Kaushik 2022)

Household adoption of rooftop solar in Karnataka is constrained by interacting informational, procedural, structural and financial frictions that persist despite a progressive policy framework. (Bagla 2026)

A qualitative study of 70 Karnataka households—24 adopters and 46 non-adopters—found that non-adopters most frequently cited roof space and roof-ownership limits as their primary barrier, followed by information shortfalls and upfront cost concerns. (Bagla 2026)

That same study measured households’ expectations and experiences of procedural complexity: prospective adopters rated expected complexity at a mean of $5.1$ out of $10$ before installation and actual experienced complexity at $2.2$ after installation, a $57$ per cent reduction. (Bagla 2026)

Adopters nevertheless reported mixed effects of subsidies: $45.8$ per cent said they would have installed even without the subsidy, while others described a “subsidy paradox” in which restrictions on panel types, vendor empanelment and paperwork diluted the subsidy’s practical value. (Bagla 2026)

Household perceptions documented in small rural case studies complement these findings: many households view solar PV as relatively cheap, easy to use and environmentally friendly, yet some perceive the technology as producing inferior quality power, vulnerable to theft, and requiring prohibitive capital outlay. (Chidembo et al. 2022)

Quantitative analyses across larger Indian samples show that perceived complexity, relative advantage, compatibility, observability and innovativeness of rooftop systems are statistically linked to purchase intentions, with trialability not predicting intention in one national study. (Kumar & Kaushik 2022)

Behavioural determinants also matter: a structural equation model using the Theory of Planned Behaviour in North Kerala found that environmental concern, awareness of government subsidies and cost–benefit perceptions positively affected attitudes, and that attitude, subjective norms and perceived behavioural control significantly predicted installation intention. (N.M & A.H 2026)

That model explained $30.3\%$ of the variance in attitude and $26.8\%$ of the variance in intention in the surveyed sample. (N.M & A.H 2026)

Context-specific surveys indicate that barriers and levers differ by place: urban residents’ responses in Patna emphasise institutional coordination and public participation as prerequisites for uptake, implying that solutions require collaboration across government, utilities and the public. (Kumar 2025)

Several studies therefore converge on a pattern: supply-side procedural simplification and clearer information reduce perceived complexity, while structural constraints (roof area, ownership) and liquidity constraints keep many households from translating willingness into installation. (Bagla 2026)(Chidembo et al. 2022)

Policy interventions should address the bundle of frictions—targeted outreach to correct quality and reliability perceptions, streamlined paperwork and broader vendor empanelment, mechanisms to relax roof-ownership and financing constraints—to align subsidy design with household realities. (Bagla 2026)(Kumar & Kaushik 2022)
